title: Where does it hurt
goal: Say what hurts, get by at the pharmacy and the doctor's — and learn one more sentence pattern that flips the subject, this time with the accusative rather than the dative.
bekal: saying what hurts with *boli me* and *bole me*
naming symptoms and asking for medicine at the pharmacy
recognizing the command forms used by doctors, shop staff and street directions

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kod doktora
dialogs.intro: Day four, and Budi's throat feels like sandpaper. Emir takes him to the nearest *Dom zdravlja* and waits outside.

lines.speaker: Doktorica:
lines.text: Dobar dan. Izvolite, sjednite. Šta vas muči?
lines.id: Good afternoon. Please, have a seat. What's troubling you?
lines.literal: good-m day. here-you-are, sit-pl. what you-pl-acc it-troubles?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Dobar dan. Boli me grlo, već tri dana.
lines.id: Good afternoon. My throat hurts, for three days now.
lines.literal: good-m day. it-hurts me-acc throat, already three day-gen.

lines.speaker: Doktorica:
lines.text: Otvorite usta i recite "a". … Grlo je crveno.
lines.id: Open your mouth and say "ah". … Your throat is red.
lines.literal: open-pl mouth and say-pl "a". … throat it-is red-n.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Boli i kad gutam. I glava me boli.
lines.id: It hurts when I swallow, too. And my head hurts.
lines.literal: it-hurts also when I-swallow. and head me-acc it-hurts.

lines.speaker: Doktorica:
lines.text: Nije ozbiljno. Obična upala grla, virusna.
lines.id: It's not serious. An ordinary sore throat, viral.
lines.literal: not-it-is serious-n. ordinary-f inflammation throat-gen, viral-f.

lines.speaker: Doktorica:
lines.text: Ne trebate. Pijte puno čaja, odmarajte se i nemojte izlaziti.
lines.id: No, you don't. Drink plenty of tea, rest and don't go out.
lines.literal: not you-pl-need. drink-pl much tea-gen, rest-pl self and don't-pl go-out.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: A mogu li raditi od kuće?
lines.id: And can I work from home?
lines.literal: and I-can whether work from home-gen?

lines.speaker: Doktorica:
lines.text: Možete, ali polako. Evo vam recept za pastile.
lines.id: You can, but take it easy. Here's a prescription for lozenges.
lines.literal: you-pl-can, but slowly. here-is to-you-pl prescription for lozenge-acc-pl.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you. When should I come back?

lines.speaker: Doktorica:
lines.text: Ako za tri dana ne bude bolje, dođite ponovo. Ozdravite brzo!

notes: ***Boli me grlo* — the subject is the throat.** Literally "the throat hurts me". So when what hurts is plural, the verb goes plural too: *bole me noge* (my legs hurt), *bole me oči* (my eyes hurt). The pattern is the same as *sviđa mi se* in Unit 13 — but note the difference: *sviđa* uses the dative (*mi*), *boli* uses the accusative (*me*). Learn them as a pair so you don't mix them up.

***Šta vas muči?* is the Bosnian doctor's standard question.** Literally "what is tormenting you?" The safest answer always starts with *Boli me…* If you don't know the name of the body part, pointing and saying *ovdje me boli* (it hurts here) is enough.

***Otvorite, recite, pijte, odmarajte se, dođite, nemojte*** — six command forms in one dialogue. At the doctor's, in shops and on the street you'll **hear** these far more often than you say them, so recognizing them is what matters most. How they're formed is in the table below.

***Kada da se vratim?*** uses the *da* + present pattern from Unit 11. In questions it means "what should I do": *Šta da radim?* (what should I do?), *Gdje da idem?* (where should I go?). Very handy when you're confused.

**The Bosnian health system.** *Dom zdravlja* is the local primary care clinic, where you register and see a *porodični ljekar* (family doctor). A hospital is a *bolnica*; emergency services are *hitna pomoć*, number **124**. Pharmacies (*apoteka*) sell many medicines without a prescription and the pharmacists are used to giving advice — for minor complaints, go there first before seeing a doctor.

grammars.title: Boli me — and talking about how you feel
body: A group of health expressions uses the subject-flipping pattern. Learn the whole sentences; all you need to change is the body part.
after: **Two similar patterns with different cases — don't mix them up.** *Boli **me*** uses the **accusative** (*me, te, ga, je, nas, vas, ih*): the body is hurting me. *Sviđa **mi** se* and *hladno **mi** je* use the **dative** (*mi, ti, mu, joj, nam, vam, im*). A way to remember: pain attacks you (accusative); feelings and impressions come to you (dative).

**There's also a second way, with a noun:** *Imam glavobolju* (I have a headache), *imam zubobolju* (toothache), *imam stomakobolju* (stomachache). This form is a bit more formal and common on forms; in conversation, *boli me* is the usual choice.
**To ask someone else**, just swap the pronoun: *Šta te boli?* (what hurts?), *Boli li vas?* (does it hurt?), *Da li ga još boli?* (does he still have pain?).
**Phrases you must have:** *Ozdravi!* / *Ozdravite!* (get well soon — informal / polite), *Brzo ozdravljenje!* (speedy recovery), and what Bosnians say most often when someone sneezes: *Nazdravlje!*

grammars.title: The imperative — command forms
body: You'll hear these more often than you say them, so the learning order is: recognize first, use later. They're built from the *oni* form, not the dictionary form.
after: **How: take the *oni* form, drop the ending, then add.** If what's left ends in a consonant, add **-i**: *piš- → piši*, *dođ- → dođi*, *otvor- → otvori*. If it ends in a vowel, add **-j**: *pi- → pij*, *čita- → čitaj*, *da- → daj*. For the polite form just add **-te**.

**Prohibitions don't use this form.** Instead you use *nemoj* (informal) or *nemojte* (polite) + dictionary form: *Nemoj zaboraviti! Nemojte izlaziti!* The form *ne pij* does exist, but it sounds harsh, like a military order — *nemoj piti* is much more natural.

**Commands you'll hear most on the street:** *Izvolite!* (here you go, please), *Sjednite!* (sit down), *Uđite!* (come in), *Idite pravo!* (go straight on), *Sačekajte, molim!* (wait a moment, please), *Požurite!* (hurry up).
**"Let's" is formed with the ending *-mo*:** *Idemo!* (let's go), *Nađimo se u sedam* (let's meet at seven), *Popijmo kafu* (let's have a coffee). And the most common of all: *Hajdemo!*

sections.title: Tijelo i zdravlje — body, symptoms, pharmacy

blocks.text: The first table covers body parts. Remember: the body part is the **subject** in a *boli me* sentence, so what you need is the dictionary form, not an object form — which makes this easier than it looks.

head: At the pharmacy
English
rows: Do you have anything for a headache?
I need something for a cough.
Do you have this without a prescription?

blocks.title: Two words that work harder than you'd think
items: ***Ruka*** means hand **and** arm at once; ***noga*** means foot **and** leg. Bosnian doesn't separate them, which takes some getting used to for English speakers. If you need to be precise: *šaka* (hand), *stopalo* (foot).

***Srce*** means the heart as an organ and as the seat of feelings — just like English *heart*. *Boli me srce* can mean either, and context tells you which. If you want to be sure you're not misunderstood at the doctor's, describe the symptoms.

I read a little every evening.
I worked on it, but didn't get it done.
When I've finished, I'll let you know.
